name: Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning

clinicalPearls: Diarrhea is defined as the passage of three or more loose or watery stools (conforming to the shape of the container) within a 24-hour period; illness lasting more than 2 weeks is generally classified as chronic and shifts the likely differential away from typical acute infectious causes (Harrison 22e p.1078, 1079).

The first practical step is to separate noninflammatory from inflammatory disease: watery diarrhea with no fecal leukocytes and minimal/no fecal lactoferrin points to proximal small-bowel enterotoxin-mediated disease, whereas fecal polymorphonuclear leukocytes and high fecal lactoferrin point to colonic invasion or cytotoxin (dysentery/inflammatory diarrhea) (Harrison 22e p.1077-1079).

Infective dose varies enormously and shapes transmission: as few as 10-100 organisms/cysts of Shigella, enterohemorrhagic E. coli, Giardia, or Entamoeba cause infection and allow person-to-person spread, while 10^5-10^8 Vibrio cholerae must be ingested, often requiring growth in food first (Harrison 22e p.1076).

Neurotoxin-mediated food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus emetic form) is caused by toxin preformed outside the host, giving the shortest incubation (1-6 h), prominent vomiting, and usually no fever (Harrison 22e p.1076-1077, 1080).

Stool appearance is diagnostically informative: bloody/mucoid stool suggests large-bowel ulceration/inflammation; profuse rice-water stools suggest cholera or a similar toxigenic process; bulky white/gray stools suggest a malabsorptive small-bowel process (Harrison 22e p.1078).
Bloody stools WITHOUT fecal leukocytes should specifically raise suspicion for Shiga toxin-producing enterohemorrhagic E. coli (e.g., O157:H7) (Harrison 22e p.1078).

Severity is judged largely by dehydration: thirst and dry mouth indicate mild dehydration; orthostatic blood-pressure fall, skin tenting, and sunken eyes/fontanelle indicate moderate dehydration; lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock indicate severe dehydration (Harrison 22e p.1078).

Recent or current antibiotic use shifts suspicion toward Clostridioides difficile; C. difficile is the predominant cause of nosocomial diarrhea in U.S. adults, and stool culture for other pathogens in the hospital setting is low-yield (Harrison 22e p.1078-1080).

Host defenses against enteric pathogens include the intestinal microbiota (colonization resistance, >99% anaerobic colonic flora with acidic pH/volatile fatty acids), gastric acid, peristalsis, the mucus barrier, mucosal/secretory IgA immunity, and host genetics (Harrison 22e p.1077).
Blood group O confers increased susceptibility to disease from V. cholerae, Shigella, E. coli O157, and norovirus (Harrison 22e p.1077).

Salmonella Typhi and Yersinia enterocolitica can penetrate intact mucosa, multiply in Peyer patches/lymph nodes, and disseminate to cause enteric fever - fever, headache, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, splenomegaly, and leukopenia (Harrison 22e p.1077).

Cholera toxin is the prototype enterotoxin: its A subunit ADP-ribosylates a GTP-binding protein, persistently activating adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, increasing Cl- secretion and decreasing Na+ absorption to drive secretory diarrhea; E. coli LT acts identically, while ST acts via guanylate cyclase and cyclic GMP (Harrison 22e p.1076-1077).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute infectious diarrhea results from a contest between ingested enteric pathogens and host defenses. Pathogens overcome defenses through small infective inoculum, adherence/colonization factors (e.g., V. cholerae toxin-coregulated pilus; enterotoxigenic E. coli colonization factor antigen; attaching-effacing lesions of enteropathogenic and enterohemorrhagic E. coli), and the elaboration of toxins or direct invasion. Three broad mechanisms produce three clinical patterns: (1) Noninflammatory enterotoxin-mediated disease in the proximal small bowel causes watery diarrhea without fecal leukocytes - the cholera-toxin/LT pathway elevates cyclic AMP (increased Cl- secretion, decreased Na+ absorption) and ST elevates cyclic GMP. (2) Inflammatory disease in the colon/distal small bowel results from cytotoxins (e.g., Shiga toxin of S. dysenteriae type 1 and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, V. parahaemolyticus, C. difficile) or from mucosal invasion (Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Salmonella), producing dysentery with fecal leukocytes and blood. (3) Penetrating organisms (Salmonella Typhi, Y. enterocolitica) traverse intact mucosa, multiply in lymphoid tissue, and disseminate to cause enteric fever. Neurotoxins (staphylococcal, B. cereus emetic) are typically preformed outside the host and act on the nervous system to cause rapid-onset vomiting. Host protection depends on the intestinal microbiota's colonization resistance, gastric acidity, intestinal motility/peristalsis, the mucin barrier, mucosal and systemic immunity, and genetic factors; impairment of any of these (achlorhydria/acid suppression, antimotility drugs, antibiotic-altered flora, immunocompromise) raises infection risk and severity.
additionalDifferentials: Noninflammatory watery diarrhea: enterotoxigenic and enteroaggregative E. coli, Vibrio cholerae, Clostridium perfringens, Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus, Aeromonas hydrophila, Plesiomonas shigelloides, rotavirus, norovirus, enteric adenovirus, Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, microsporidia

Inflammatory diarrhea/dysentery: Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, enterohemorrhagic E. coli, enteroinvasive E. coli, Yersinia enterocolitica, Listeria monocytogenes, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, Clostridioides difficile, Entamoeba histolytica, Klebsiella oxytoca
Enteric fever (penetrating): Salmonella Typhi, Yersinia enterocolitica
Traveler's diarrhea: most often enterotoxigenic and enteroaggregative E. coli, with Campylobacter jejuni notably common in Asia
Nonbacterial / noninfectious food poisoning: capsaicin (hot peppers) and fish/shellfish toxins
infectionMimics: Malaria (fever and diarrhea, and prominent vomiting, may occur with infection outside the GI tract)
Clostridioides difficile / antibiotic-associated colitis in patients on or recently on antibiotics
Yersinia enterocolitica infection presenting as an appendicitis-like (pseudoappendicitis) syndrome
nonInfectiousMimics: Inflammatory bowel disease (acute diarrheal illness may be its initial presentation or an exacerbation, sometimes precipitated by traveler's diarrhea)
Noninfectious food poisoning from capsaicin and fish/shellfish toxins
additionalInvestigations: Stool examination for gross blood/mucus and a fecal leukocyte smear (thin smear + methylene blue wet mount) to identify inflammatory disease, although its predictive value is debated
Fecal lactoferrin (latex agglutination or ELISA) - a more sensitive marker of fecal leukocytes than the WBC smear

Stool culture for Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter in febrile inflammatory diarrhea (MacConkey/Salmonella-Shigella agar/selenite broth; Campylobacter requires 42 degrees C microaerophilic culture)
Selective culture for V. cholerae on TCBS or TTG agar, plus rapid diagnostic tests when cholera is suspected
Sorbitol-MacConkey culture and/or Shiga toxin/PCR testing of visibly bloody stools for E. coli O157:H7
C. difficile toxin A/B testing (enzyme immunoassay, latex agglutination, or PCR) for nosocomial or antibiotic-associated diarrhea
Rapid antigen, immunofluorescence, or PCR (and less sensitive microscopy) for Giardia, Cryptosporidium, and Entamoeba histolytica

Multiplex nucleic acid amplification panels for viral/bacterial/parasitic pathogens - faster and more sensitive than culture, but may detect multiple organisms and complicate interpretation; CDC advises follow-up culture to allow susceptibility testing and outbreak typing
redFlags: Signs of severe dehydration: lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock
Fever, which often signals invasive disease
Bloody or mucoid stools (dysentery) indicating large-bowel ulceration
Bloody stools without fecal leukocytes - alert for Shiga toxin-producing enterohemorrhagic E. coli and risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome

Diarrhea in an immunocompromised host (cell-mediated immunity defects/AIDS, hypogammaglobulinemia, cancer), where infection can be life-threatening with persistent infection, bacteremia, and metastatic seeding
Profuse rice-water stools suggesting cholera, with risk of rapid life-threatening volume loss
Diarrhea in infants <2 years with moderate dehydration, fever >24 h, bloody stools, or prolonged duration
harrison.prognosis: Most acute diarrheal episodes are mild and self-limited. Traveler's diarrhea is typically self-limited, lasting 1-5 days, and Clostridium perfringens food poisoning rarely lasts more than 24 h; toxin-mediated staphylococcal/B. cereus emetic illness generally lasts under 12 h. Globally, however, acute diarrheal disease remains a leading cause of illness, associated with an estimated 1.57 million deaths per year, and in low- and middle-income countries it accounts for about one in ten deaths in children under 5; recurrent intestinal infection contributes to stunting, wasting, micronutrient deficiency, and malnutrition. Outcome is worse in immunocompromised hosts, where dehydration can also compromise renal function and increase immunosuppressive drug toxicity. Postdiarrhea complications include chronic diarrhea (~1% of travelers; protozoa account for about one-third), postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome (~10% of those with traveler's diarrhea), reactive arthritis (especially after Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia), hemolytic-uremic syndrome (Shiga toxin-producing bacteria), and Guillain-Barre syndrome (especially after Campylobacter).
pitfalls: Relying on the fecal leukocyte smear alone - its predictive value is debated, and fecal lactoferrin is more sensitive (Harrison 22e p.1079).

Routine stool culture cannot distinguish pathogenic E. coli from normal flora, and enterotoxin assays are unavailable in most clinical labs, so a negative routine culture does not exclude E. coli disease (Harrison 22e p.1080).
Sending broad stool cultures for nosocomial diarrhea is low-yield and not cost-effective; initial workup should focus on C. difficile (Harrison 22e p.1080).

Antimotility agents (e.g., diphenoxylate-atropine) and opioids can prolong fever and organism shedding in Shigella infection and increase bacteremia risk in Salmonella - impaired motility favors bacterial overgrowth (Harrison 22e p.1077).

Multiplex NAAT panels may detect multiple pathogens, complicating interpretation, and the absence of an isolate prevents susceptibility testing and outbreak typing - CDC advises follow-up culture (Harrison 22e p.1080).
Reheating/frying contaminated fried rice may not destroy preformed heat-stable B. cereus toxin or its heat-resistant spores (Harrison 22e p.1080).
Missing infection outside the GI tract (e.g., malaria) as a cause of fever and diarrhea/vomiting (Harrison 22e p.1078).
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is graded clinically by degree of dehydration (Harrison 22e p.1078). Mild dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, decreased axillary sweat, decreased urine output, slight weight loss. Moderate dehydration: orthostatic fall in blood pressure, skin tenting, sunken eyes (or sunken fontanelle in infants). Severe dehydration: lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock. The complementary classification is mechanistic/syndromic per Table 138-1: noninflammatory (enterotoxin, proximal small bowel, watery diarrhea, no fecal leukocytes), inflammatory (invasion or cytotoxin, colon/distal small bowel, dysentery, fecal PMNs and high lactoferrin), and penetrating (distal small bowel, enteric fever, fecal mononuclear cells).
